# Fresh19 negative controls and disposition

Author: /root/round211_functional_surgery_residual.
Claim status: PROVABLE AS STATED for the elementary controls below under
their stated assumptions. A fresh two-axis candidate is NOT CURRENTLY
JUSTIFIED. These are source-subtraction deductions, not independent review.
No scientific program, pilot, enumeration or experiment was run.

Dependency map: fixed local group actions consume fixed-word recurrence
and inversion; an antitone adjunction consumes conjugation recurrence;
named metric trimming supplies descent and core/forest structure; named
Whitehead minimization supplies length descent. These four source directions
are not four newly instantiated literal systems.

## 1. Fixed vertex flips: group action, not a residual clock

For a fixed finite ground set V, encode a set family by membership bits.
On the pair indexed by Z and Z minus {j}, in that order with j in Z,
twist and loop-complement use respectively

    A* = [[0,1],[1,0]],    A+ = [[1,1],[0,1]]  over F_2.

The matrices generate GL_2(F_2), isomorphic to S_3. Operations at distinct
coordinates commute. Thus a fixed word of these operations is one fixed
element of S_3^V, whose sixth power is identity. Every state is recurrent,
every period divides six, and each target has its unique inverse image under
the inverse group word. No new time or inverse mechanism remains.
This uses the primary Definition 4/Lemma 5 and following group calculation.
[Brijder–Hoogeboom](https://arxiv.org/html/0909.4004v4)

Carrier cautions: arbitrary delta-matroids are not closed under loop
complementation (the source's Example 10). Graph pivots require nonsingular
principal sets. This desk does not totalize a partial graph operation.

Old B2B-09 has a fixed invertible principal block and is involutive; it is
not asserted identical to every set-system word. More importantly, old C04
already selects partial-dual edges from current boundary-length parity.
That selector is state-dependent, so the fixed-word sixth-power argument
does NOT kill C04. C04 is an exact old rule, not a fresh opening here.
No selector is invented to evade the fixed-word exclusion.

## 2. Isbell conjugation: the antitone identity is already available

For a finite symmetric metric d and nonnegative real-valued f, write

    Qf(i) = max_j max(d(i,j)-f(j),0).

This is the symmetric coordinate form of the source's L/R adjunction.
It reverses pointwise numeric order. For each i,j,

    Qf(j) >= d(j,i)-f(i),

so d(i,j)-Qf(j) <= f(i); taking the positive maximum gives
Q^2 f <= f. Applying Q reverses this inequality and yields Q^3 f >= Qf.
Applying Q^2 g <= g to g=Qf yields the reverse. Therefore Q^3=Q.

Consequently the image is Fix(Q^2), with entry in at most one step and
period one or two. This is not necessarily Fix(Q): for a two-point
distance-one space, (0,0) and (1,1) form a strict two-cycle. The classical
tight-span fixed equation is Qf=f, whereas the Isbell completion uses
conjugate pairs. The source distinguishes these spaces.
[Willerton, sections 2.1, 3.1 and 4.1](https://arxiv.org/html/1302.4370v1)

This calculation is on a named real-valued operator, not the registration
of a new finite grid literal. No rounding, grid closure, selector, inverse
count or sharp finite-carrier extremum is introduced. P106 uses subset
polarity, DHC first selects a farthest-subset radius, and OF-K uses two
registers. They are not literally Q; their generic polarity mechanism is
the relevant warning. No all-carrier conjugacy is claimed.

## 3. Metric trimming: source-owned descent; finiteness must be proved

For at least three points, let

    p(x) = min_{y,z distinct from x and each other}
                 (d(x,y)+d(x,z)-d(y,z))/2.

For two points p is half their distance; for one point p=0. Subtract
p(x)+p(y) off the off-diagonal distances and quotient zero distances.
This is the named trimming t(X). Its iterates reach a trim core in at most
|X| steps; the source supplies the canonical metric forest connecting X
to that core, and the converse trim-base forest theorem.
[Turaev, sections 2–5](https://arxiv.org/html/1612.06760v1)

“Finite metric space” fixes the number of points, not a finite number of
possible metrics. Nor is the naive integer-distance carrier closed.
A direct hand calculation illustrates this; it is not a numerical run.
Take four points with

    d12=d13=d14=d34=2,    d23=d24=3.

Every triangle has side lengths (2,2,3), (2,2,2), or (3,3,2), so this is a
metric. The three Gromov products at points 1,2,3,4 have minima
1/2,3/2,1,1, respectively. After subtraction the pairs 12 and 34 have
distance zero and every cross distance is 1/2. The quotient is therefore
a two-point metric at distance 1/2, outside the integer-distance carrier.
Its next trim is a singleton. This refutes only naive closure, not every
possible finite discretization.

The Manhattan primary paper identifies trimming with its metric-center
set by an isometry (Theorem 1). Even there the two-point center convention
can leave the integer-coordinate plane: {(0,0),(1,0)} maps to {(1/2,0)}.
The source's identification is not a new inverse/fibre theorem.
[Çakmak–Deniz–Koçak, Definition 2 and Theorem 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2306.05822v1)

Old RNG/strong-resolution graph reconstruction is not asserted identical
to trimming. Source ownership of descent/core reconstruction and absence
of a separate evaluated inverse/extremum suffice to reject a proposal at
this desk. No padded state space or discretization is designed to rescue it.

## 4. Whitehead minimization: named descent, not free cancellation

The read publisher introduction states the classical Whitehead reduction
criterion for cyclically reduced words: a word that is not length-minimal
in its automorphism orbit admits a length-decreasing Whitehead move.
Repeatedly apply such a move and cyclically reduce. Each nonterminal
invocation strictly decreases the nonnegative integer cyclic length, so
there are at most the initial length many decreasing invocations.
This is the standard minimization phase, not a claim about the entire
Whitehead decision algorithm's running time.
[Kapovich–Schupp–Shpilrain, Convention 1.1, Proposition 1.2 and following algorithm](https://msp.org/pjm/2006/223-1/pjm-v223-n1-p06-s.pdf)

A deterministic tie convention was not chosen or instantiated. Neither an
exact statewise iteration clock nor an evaluated all-target fibre/extremum
is proved. The source's generic-case results are not upgraded to all-input
dynamics, and the original 1936 proof is not represented as read.

Old D6 deletes the leftmost adjacent inverse pair and has clock
(|w|-|red(w)|)/2. Its endpoint agrees with parallel free reduction, although
the one-step schedules differ. Whitehead automorphisms can alter a reduced
word without representing the same group element, so D6 is not the
Whitehead update and its exact deletion clock cannot be transferred.
The decisive exclusion here is named length-minimization ownership and
missing independent residual value, not a false literal identity.

## 5. Admission outcome and limits

| Source direction | Temporal residual | Independent inverse/extremal residual | Desk result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fixed set-system flip word | Consumed by the fixed group element | Unique group inverse is consumed | No proposal |
| Isbell conjugation | Consumed by the antitone adjunction | None evaluated | No proposal |
| Metric trimming / Manhattan center representation | Named trimming descent already owned | Core/forest representation is owned; no new evaluated fibre theorem | No proposal |
| Whitehead minimization | Named integer length descent | None evaluated | No proposal |

No line asserts universal exhaustion of these fields, global priority, or
that a genuinely different intrinsic map could never be interesting.
The concrete result is ZERO_NEW_LITERALS / ZERO_PILOT_PROPOSALS /
ZERO_EXECUTED / ZERO_NOMINATIONS / ZERO_RESERVES / NO_FRESH_SLATE.
Only root may integrate this author desk into the central batch/recovery
indices after its own intake. Historical and frozen records remain intact.

An elementary cancellation deletes $aa^{-1}$. Any two cancellations from
one word have the following diamond. Disjoint pairs can both be deleted in
either order with the same resulting word. Overlapping pairs form

## Assumptions and notation

Graphs are finite, simple, undirected and labelled. For fixed $n\ge1$, let
$\mathcal G_n^c$ be all connected graphs on $[n]$ with unit edge lengths.
$d_G$ is shortest-path distance; $N_G(u)$ and $N_G[u]$ are open and closed
neighborhoods. Complementation retains all labels and has no loops.

For a finite metric $d$ on $V$, define $R(d)$ by, for distinct $u,v$,
$$uv\in E(R(d))\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
d(u,v)\le\max\{d(u,x),d(v,x)\}\quad\text{for every }x\in V.$$
The weak inequality, including ties, is the source convention. Define
$T(G)=R(d_G)$ on $\mathcal G_n^c$.

For connected $G$, define $F(G)$ on the full label set by joining distinct
$u,v$ exactly when both conditions hold:
$$d_G(v,w)\le d_G(u,v)\quad(\forall w\in N_G(u)),\qquad
d_G(u,w)\le d_G(u,v)\quad(\forall w\in N_G(v)).$$
These are mutually maximally distant vertices. This is the source's
$G_{SR+I}$ convention, not its boundary-only $G_{SR}$ convention.

For an odd integer $q\ge3$ and an invertible residue $s\bmod q$, let
$C(q,s)$ have vertex set $\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z$ and edges
$\{i,i+s\}$ for every $i$. Put $k=(q-1)/2$. Let $D$ be the old
degree-two neighbor-pair shortcut, restricted here to these cycles.

## Proof strategy and dependency map

1. RNG identity: positive integral distances retain edges; an internal
   shortest-path point excludes each nonedge. No external theorem needed.
2. Diameter-two formula: distance-two pairs are maximal; adjacent maximal
   pairs are exactly true twins. This rederives the read primary Proposition 14.
3. Odd cycles: identify the maximally distant positions, then calculate
   labelled step multiplication. The actual old proof supplies $D:s\mapsto2s$.
4. Scope checks: explicit $C_4$ and four-vertex paw calculations. No
   extrapolation from graph isomorphism or a pilot is used.

## Proof

### 1. RNG identity on the whole connected unit-graph carrier

Step 1. If $uv$ is an edge, $d_G(u,v)=1$. For $x=u$ or $x=v$ the maximum
in the definition is $1$. For any other $x$, both distances are positive
integers, so the maximum is at least $1$. Thus every edge is retained.

Step 2. If distinct $u,v$ are nonadjacent, set $m=d_G(u,v)\ge2$.
Take a shortest path $u=x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_m=v$ and choose $x=x_{m-1}$.
The shortest-path subpath property gives $d_G(u,x)=m-1$ and $d_G(v,x)=1$.
Both are less than $m$, so this $x$ violates the RNG inequality. No nonedge
is introduced. Hence $T(G)=G$.

Step 3. For $n=1$, there are no vertex pairs and the same equality holds.
Thus $T$ is an endomorphism of $\mathcal G_n^c$, every state is fixed,
and for every target $H\in\mathcal G_n^c$, $T^{-1}(H)=\{H\}$.
This is an identity control, not a temporal contribution. Arbitrary
real-valued metric spaces are not silently substituted as a finite carrier.

### 2. Diameter-two strong resolution: known exact formula

Assume $G$ is connected of diameter exactly two.

Step 1. A nonedge $uv$ has distance two. Every distance in the two maximality
tests is at most two, so $u,v$ are mutually maximally distant.

Step 2. If $uv$ is an edge, the maximality of $u$ from $v$ is equivalent to
$N_G(u)\subseteq N_G[v]$. Mutual maximality gives both corresponding
inclusions, and, since $u,v$ are adjacent, these are equivalent to
$N_G[u]=N_G[v]$. Conversely that equality makes both tests hold.

Step 3. True-twin equality partitions vertices into classes, and each
non-singleton class is a clique of $G$. Therefore
$$E(F(G))=E(\overline G)\ \cup
\{uv:u\ne v,\ N_G[u]=N_G[v]\}.$$
In particular, if $G$ is true-twin-free, $F(G)=\overline G$. This is the
full-label form of the primary source's Proposition 14; deleting its isolated
vertices gives that source's boundary-only version. It is not asserted that
all diameter-two inputs have diameter-two or connected outputs.

### 3. Exact inverse collision on labelled odd cycles

Step 1. Since $s$ is invertible, positions $i+js$ give cyclic order in
$C(q,s)$. Distances from position $0$ are $\min(j,q-j)$, whose maximum is
$k$. At either maximum position $k$ or $k+1$, each neighbor has distance at
most $k$. At a distinct nonmaximum position, one neighbor increases the
distance by one. Consequently two distinct vertices are mutually maximally
distant exactly when their cyclic separation is $k$.

Step 2. It follows as an equality of labelled edge sets that
$$F(C(q,s))=C(q,ks).$$
The integer $k$ is coprime to $q$, because any common divisor divides both
$q$ and $2k=q-1$. Hence the output remains in this restricted class.
